subject: physics

items.q: Which phrase best describes all electromagnetic waves?
items.correct: Transverse waves that transfer energy to an absorber
items.misconception: Longitudinal waves that transfer energy to an absorber
items.why: Sound is usually the first wave studied in depth, and both sound and light travel outwards from a source, so the type of oscillation is assumed to be the same. Sound is longitudinal, but every electromagnetic wave is transverse: the oscillation is at right angles to the direction in which the energy is transferred, not along it.
items.random_wrong: Transverse waves that transfer matter to any absorber

items.q: A radio transmitter sends radio waves to the aerial of a car radio. Which statement describes the energy transfer?
items.correct: Energy is transferred from the transmitter to the aerial.
items.misconception: Energy is transferred from the aerial to the transmitter.
items.why: Phrases such as 'the plant takes in sunlight' or 'the aerial picks up the signal' put the absorber in the active role, hiding the direction of the transfer. The wave is emitted by the source and carries energy away from it; the absorber receives that energy. Naming the source and the absorber separately for each example fixes the direction.
items.random_wrong: No energy is transferred, only information is carried.

items.q: Which statement about the speed of electromagnetic waves is correct?
items.correct: All types travel at the same velocity through a vacuum.
items.misconception: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum.
items.why: Students link 'high frequency' and 'high energy' with 'fast', because in everyday language something high-frequency sounds rapid, and because dangerous things are imagined as fast-moving. Speed is the same for every group in a vacuum or air. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency. A radio wave and a gamma ray leaving a distant star together arrive at the Earth together.
items.random_wrong: Radio waves travel faster than gamma rays in a vacuum.

items.q: Ultraviolet and infrared leave the Sun at the same moment and travel through space to the Earth. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: They arrive together because both travel at the same speed.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet arrives first because its frequency is higher.
items.why: Students link 'high frequency' and 'high energy' with 'fast', because in everyday language something high-frequency sounds rapid, and because dangerous things are imagined as fast-moving. Speed is the same for every group in a vacuum or air. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency. A radio wave and a gamma ray leaving a distant star together arrive at the Earth together.
items.random_wrong: Infrared arrives first because its wavelength is longer.

items.q: The electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous. What does this tell you?
items.correct: There are no gaps between the groups of waves in it.
items.misconception: There are exactly seven separate wave types, with gaps.
items.why: Textbook diagrams draw the spectrum as seven coloured boxes with hard lines between them, which looks like seven separate things rather than one unbroken range. The spectrum is continuous. The seven names label regions of a single unbroken range of wavelengths, and the boundaries are not sharp — waves exist at every wavelength in between.
items.random_wrong: The waves are all given out continuously and never stop.

items.q: Which list of groups is in order from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength?
items.correct: microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet
items.misconception: microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, visible light
items.why: Infrared and ultraviolet are often taught together as 'the invisible ones near light', and their positions are then swapped or merged. The order is infrared, then visible light, then ultraviolet. The prefixes help: infra means below the red end and ultra means beyond the violet end, so ultraviolet lies past violet, not before red.

items.q: A group of the electromagnetic spectrum has a lower frequency than infrared. Which group could it be?
items.correct: microwaves
items.misconception: ultraviolet
items.why: Infrared and ultraviolet are often taught together as 'the invisible ones near light', and their positions are then swapped or merged. The order is infrared, then visible light, then ultraviolet. The prefixes help: infra means below the red end and ultra means beyond the violet end, so ultraviolet lies past violet, not before red.

items.q: Compared with visible light, radio waves have:
items.correct: a longer wavelength and a lower frequency
items.misconception: a longer wavelength and a higher frequency
items.why: 'Longer' and 'higher' both feel like 'more', so students expect the two quantities to increase together instead of running in opposite directions. The specification orders the spectrum from long to short wavelength, which is the same order as low to high frequency. Radio waves have the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency; gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency.
items.random_wrong: a shorter wavelength and a lower frequency

items.q: Which statement about the colours of visible light is correct?
items.correct: Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light.
items.misconception: Violet light has a longer wavelength than red light.
items.why: Colour is judged by how it looks rather than by its place in the spectrum, and the specification's own phrase 'red to violet' is read without noticing that it runs long to short. The specification lists visible light as 'red to violet' inside a run from long to short wavelength. Red therefore has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency of the visible colours, and violet the shortest and highest.
items.random_wrong: Red light has a higher frequency than violet light.

items.q: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum can the human eye detect?
items.correct: Visible light only, a limited range of the spectrum.
items.misconception: Visible light and infrared, which we feel as warmth.
items.why: Warmth from a fire is felt at the same time as its glow is seen, so detecting infrared with the skin gets confused with seeing it. The skin senses the warming caused by absorbed infrared; the eye does not detect infrared at all. The glow of a fire that we do see is visible light. That is why an infrared remote control beam is invisible.
items.random_wrong: Every group in the spectrum, from radio to gamma rays.

items.q: A television remote control sends out infrared. Why can you not see the beam?
items.correct: Your eyes detect only visible light, not infrared.
items.misconception: The infrared beam is too dim for your eyes to detect.
items.why: Warmth from a fire is felt at the same time as its glow is seen, so detecting infrared with the skin gets confused with seeing it. The skin senses the warming caused by absorbed infrared; the eye does not detect infrared at all. The glow of a fire that we do see is visible light. That is why an infrared remote control beam is invisible.
items.random_wrong: Infrared travels too quickly for your eyes to detect.

items.q: Food placed in a microwave oven becomes hotter. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Microwaves transfer energy from the oven to the food.
items.misconception: Microwaves transfer heated matter into the food.
items.why: Everyday transfers involve something physically arriving — post, water, hot air — so students expect a wave to deliver a substance too. Electromagnetic waves transfer energy, not matter. The evidence that something arrived is the change in the absorber, such as its temperature rising or a current appearing in it.
items.random_wrong: The food absorbs hot air produced inside the oven.

items.q: Sunlight falls on a solar cell and the cell produces electricity. In this energy transfer, the absorber is:
items.correct: the solar cell, which takes in the light
items.misconception: the Sun, which gives out the light
items.why: Phrases such as 'the plant takes in sunlight' or 'the aerial picks up the signal' put the absorber in the active role, hiding the direction of the transfer. The wave is emitted by the source and carries energy away from it; the absorber receives that energy. Naming the source and the absorber separately for each example fixes the direction.

items.q: Which statement about radio waves transferring energy is correct?
items.correct: An aerial absorbs them, so energy reaches the aerial.
items.misconception: They carry information only, so no energy is transferred.
items.why: Radio waves produce no sensation at all, so there is nothing to feel, and the everyday word for what they do is 'carry a signal' rather than 'transfer energy'. A receiving aerial absorbs radio waves and an alternating current appears in it. That current is evidence that energy has been transferred from the transmitter to the aerial.
items.random_wrong: They transfer energy only once they slow down in air.

items.q: The waves of the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of which two properties?
items.correct: wavelength and frequency
items.misconception: wavelength and velocity
items.why: Students link 'high frequency' and 'high energy' with 'fast', because in everyday language something high-frequency sounds rapid, and because dangerous things are imagined as fast-moving. Speed is the same for every group in a vacuum or air. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency. A radio wave and a gamma ray leaving a distant star together arrive at the Earth together.

items.q: A camper holds their hands near a fire and feels them get warmer. Which pair names the source and the absorber correctly?
items.correct: source: the fire; absorber: the camper's hands
items.misconception: source: the camper's hands; absorber: the flames
items.why: Phrases such as 'the plant takes in sunlight' or 'the aerial picks up the signal' put the absorber in the active role, hiding the direction of the transfer. The wave is emitted by the source and carries energy away from it; the absorber receives that energy. Naming the source and the absorber separately for each example fixes the direction.
items.random_wrong: source: the hot air; absorber: the camper's hands

items.q: Can electromagnetic waves travel through empty space?
items.correct: Yes. They travel through a vacuum (space) as well as through air.
items.misconception: Waves need something to travel through, so light must need air — there must be some very thin air out in space carrying it.
items.why: Sound, water waves and waves on a rope are met first, and every one of them needs a substance. The rule 'a wave needs a medium' is over-generalised to light. Electromagnetic waves are the exception: they travel through a vacuum. Sunlight, infrared and ultraviolet cross millions of kilometres of empty space to reach the Earth, which they could not do if a substance were needed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How much of the electromagnetic spectrum can our eyes detect?
items.correct: Only visible light — a limited range of electromagnetic waves.
items.misconception: We can see most of the spectrum, because we can see light and we can also feel and sense the other waves around us.
items.why: Diagrams often draw visible light as a wide band across the middle of the spectrum, and 'sensing' warmth or sunburn gets muddled with 'seeing'. Our eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves. Everything else — radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays — is invisible to us and needs a detector.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is infrared radiation?
items.correct: It is a group of the electromagnetic spectrum — a transverse wave that transfers energy from a source to an absorber.
items.misconception: Infrared is the hot air coming off something hot; it is heat itself rather than a wave.
items.why: Infrared is met through the warmth felt near a fire or a heater, where hot air really is rising as well, so the wave and the moving hot air get merged into one idea. Infrared is an electromagnetic wave and needs no air at all. Infrared from the Sun crosses a vacuum to reach us, and a person standing to one side of a fire, not above it, still feels the energy arriving.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which comes last in the spectrum, X-rays or gamma rays?
items.correct: Gamma rays — the order ends ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
items.misconception: Gamma rays come before X-rays, because gamma is the one you meet first when learning about radioactivity.
items.why: In radioactivity the emissions are ordered alpha, beta, gamma, so gamma is remembered as a familiar early item, and the alphabet puts X near the end of the list. Learn the specification order as one list: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma rays sit at the short wavelength, high frequency end.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do electromagnetic waves travel faster in air than in a vacuum?
items.correct: No. They travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.
items.misconception: Air helps to carry the wave along, so waves must go faster in air than in empty space.
items.why: For sound, a medium is essential, so air is thought of as the thing that carries a wave rather than as something a wave passes through. The specification states that all types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air. Air is not needed and does not speed the wave up.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does it mean to say the electromagnetic spectrum is continuous?
items.correct: There are no gaps in it — waves exist at every wavelength across the whole range.
items.misconception: It means the waves are given out continuously, without stopping.
items.why: 'Continuous' in everyday use describes something going on in time, so it is read as a statement about emission rather than about the range of wavelengths. Here 'continuous' describes the range of wavelengths and frequencies, not the timing. The spectrum runs unbroken from the longest wavelengths to the shortest, whether or not any source is switched on.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
